title: Read and record a timed thermometer measurement
instruction: Wait for the desk timer to count down to zero. Use the left wrist camera to read the temperature of the thermometer suspended in the beaker. Then close the right gripper and use its fingertips to enter the measured temperature in degrees Celsius on the calculator, followed by the equals key. The timer is already running. Keep the thermometer suspended in the water. Complete the task within 120 seconds.
context: Timed laboratory measurements require an operator to wait for the specified interval, inspect an analog instrument without disturbing its probe, and record the measured value. This task combines close visual reading with numeric data entry.
setup: Dual YAM arms face a 1.10 x 1.30 m table. Left: a 250 x 150 mm steel stand base, 440 x 12 mm upright and metal screw/spring clamp with a 120 mm arm support a 320 x 9 mm glass thermometer in a 500 mL glass beaker (120 mm high, 90 mm diameter) of pink water. Right rear: a 140 x 145 mm plastic timer. Right front: a 101.6 x 139.7 mm plastic calculator with 21 keys. Initially the timer runs at 00:15; temperature rises from 35 to 45 C over 15 s and holds.
scoring: Binary score: 1 if the calculator's latest equals-key submission is 45 degrees Celsius within the trial limit; otherwise 0. Input comes from measured physical button travel. No partial credit.
run_limit: 2,400 control steps (120 simulation seconds at 20 Hz), including observation preroll. Network waits pause physics.
reset_notes: Fixed layout, seed 0. Settle mechanics for two seconds, then reset the timer to a running 00:15, thermometer to 35 C, and calculator to 0.
fidelity: CPU PhysX at 240 Hz with native YAM control at 20 Hz. The free clamp uses screw coupling, spring jaws and contact friction. Keys are spring joints; displays and the red column are geometry. Water is a fixed visual volume and heating is prescribed, without fluid or heat-transfer simulation. Material and spring values are engineering approximations.
scores: Dream-1 beta: 0.0/1.0 in 120 s, no submission. Open-loop demo: 1.0/1.0 in 40.2 s, submitted 45.
